title: The Treaty That Said 'Due North or South' #shorts
summary: The Convention of 1818 ran the border due north or south from the northwest point of the Lake of the Woods to the 49th parallel; when the point was fixed, the line ran south and left the Northwest Angle in the US.
sources: Convention of 1818 (signed London, 20 Oct 1818), Article II: a line drawn from the most North Western Point of the Lake of the Woods due north or south, as the case may be, to the 49th parallel, then west along it (Avalon Project, Yale Law School): https://avalon.law.yale.edu/19th_century/conv1818.asp

International Boundary Commission, History: 1783 line to the north-westernmost point of Lake of the Woods and thence due west to the Mississippi; 1818 Article II north or south to the 49th parallel; 1842 Webster-Ashburton Treaty settled the line to the north-westernmost point of Lake of the Woods; 1846 along the 49th parallel to the Strait of Georgia: https://internationalboundarycommission.org/en/about/history.php

Minnesota Historical Society, MNopedia, Northwest Angle: farther north than any other part of the contiguous United States; the 1783 line followed John Mitchell's map of an egg-shaped Lake of the Woods; in 1798 David Thompson proved the northernmost source of the Mississippi was south of Lake of the Woods; in 1825 Johann Ludwig Tiarks determined the northwesternmost point at the head of Angle Inlet; 1842 treaty confirmed the point: https://mnopedia.org/node/6088

Map data: Natural Earth (public domain) https://www.naturalearthdata.com and US Census Bureau cartographic boundary files (public domain) https://www.census.gov/geographies/mapping-files/time-series/geo/carto-boundary-file.html; drive and boat routes are drawn schematically

scenes.narration: In {1818|eighteen eighteen}, a treaty said: run a line due north or south to the {49th parallel|forty-ninth parallel}.
North or south, because nobody had fixed that point yet.
In {1825|eighteen twenty-five}, an astronomer did, at the head of Angle Inlet, north of the {49th|forty-ninth}.
So the line drops south, and the land east of it stays American.
In {1842|eighteen forty-two}, the Webster-Ashburton Treaty locked it in.
